I just feel more comfortable saying EYE-bee-PROE-fen. A lot of people say EYE-bee-PROE-fen instead of EYE-bue-PROE-fen. That doesn't make it right, but I'm happy to say that both variations sound about the same when said quickly. Pick your pronunciation, and own it when you say it! b863877814d58d95df9b98556373662e.description: This is the 79th episode in my drug pronunciation series. If you want to feel less frustrated learning drug names and sound more confident saying them, follow this series. Dextroamphetamine = DEX-troe-am-FET-a-meen DEX, as in "dexter," the Latin word meaning "right." (Right as opposed to left.) Troe, like a Trojan Horse am, as in I am an Ohio-licensed pharmacist FET, like fetch (For example, "Jack and Jill went up the hill to fetch a pail of water.") A (uh), which is a short "A" sound, like the "A" in the word "adoption" (uh) meen, as in bullies are mean. Emphasize DEX and FET. FET gets the most emphasis. Written pronunciation source: USP Dictionary Online https://links.thepharmacistsvoice.com/uspdictionaryonline Spoken pronunciation example: Merriam Webster's Online Dictionary and Tony PharmD's YouTube Channel https://links.thepharmacistsvoice.com/tonypharmddextroamphetamine Dexedrine = dek-suh-drin dek, like a deck of cards suh, like supper drin, which rhymes with thin. In the literature, no emphasis is indicated on any syllable. I tend to emphasize "dek." 9d7a55e99e28f34266397d38a7db72bb.description: Send us Fan MailJoshua plays super-sleuth to find out if Marie Antoinette really said, 'Let them eat cake.' He traces the line from Rousseau's Confessions to an 1843 French article and learns just why it stuck…especially since she’d been dead for half a century.## What You'll Learn- The famous quoted line mentions brioche, not cake.- The quote originated in Jean-Jacques Rousseau's autobiographical work called (oddly enough) Confessions, where he attributed it to an unnamed "great princess," years before Marie Antoinette even arrived in France. - Karr's 1843 article first linked the quote to Marie Antoinette, 50 years after having been executed. ## Key Claims- There are no, ninguna, aucune, koi saboot nahi hai, nenhuma prova, net nikakikh dokazatel’stv, zilch, keine credible evidence showing Marie Antoinette said it.- While in England, Rousseau wrote of the 'great princess' in France; meanwhile Marie Antoinette was still a child living in Austria.- French journalist Alphonse Karr’s 1843 article is the earliest known printed link to her. It’s also how he accidentally cemented the false connection between the quote and the late Queen Consort of France.***Interestingly, I read that Marie NEVER had any sovereign power and NEVER even ruled France.## Sources- Karr, Jean-Baptiste Alphonse. Les Guêpes, March 1843. Bibliothèque nationale de France / Gallica: https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/1

How do you say abciximab? abciximab = ab-SIX-i-mab, ab, like abdomen SIX, like the number 6 i, which is a short "I" sound, like the "I" in the word, "president" (sounds like, "ih") mab, which is the stem for monoclonal antibodies Emphasize SIX Sources: USP Dictionary Online or drugs.com When I was a hospital pharmacy intern in the 90s, I didn't know how to say abciximab. It was a relatively new drug name at the time, and I kinda spelled it out instead of saying it. I just need to hear it once. Then, I knew how to say it forevermore. Why pick abciximab for the series? Even though my sources say that abciximab (ReoPro) has been discontinued in the US, it is still discussed among healthcare professionals and mentioned in printed resources. Therefore, the pronunciation is worth knowing. You may hear someone say it during your lifetime, and this podcast episode will help you connect the printed name with the spoken name. Plus, if you spell out drug names because you don't know how to say them, you might relate to this episode. I know what it's like to feel insecure saying something I have never heard before.
